mainTopic: Carriers who break what they carry: the oath as a תקנת חכמים, איסי's rule that proof replaces an oath, porters' liability, and the new chapter on local custom in hiring workers.
overview: The amud opens by finishing the problems with the idea that the barrel-carrier's oath is about a slope. Even there, an oath only makes sense when there are no witnesses, as איסי בן יהודה learns from a פסוק. Then ר׳ חייא בר אבא, quoting ר׳ יוחנן, says the oath is a תקנת חכמים, made so that people will still agree to carry barrels for others. רבא gives its wording: 'I did not break it on purpose.' The גמרא then rereads רבי יהודה and רבי אלעזר according to this approach. Next, רבא rules twice like איסי, in the case of a barrel broken in the busy market of מחוזא and the case of 400 jugs of wine that went sour: where proof can be found, one must bring it. רב חייא בר יוסף sets a half-payment rule for porters who carry with a pole, and רב tells רבה בר בר חנן to go beyond the law with poor porters who broke his barrel. The chapter ends, and a new משנה teaches that workers' hours and food follow local custom. The גמרא explains that rule, and ריש לקיש's statement begins, continuing on the next amud.

steps.title: Even on a slope, why not just bring witnesses?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds one more problem to the earlier idea that the oath is about a slope. An oath only makes sense when there are no witnesses. If there are witnesses, the carrier should bring them and go free with no oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even in the case of a slope, this only works where there is no evidence. But where there is evidence, let him bring evidence and be exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its list of problems with the earlier explanation of רבי מאיר's oath. It points out that even the 'slope' explanation only works when nobody saw what happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the גמרא suggested the oath is limited to a slippery slope, where breaking the barrel is not the carrier's fault. Now it narrows that further. Swearing only makes sense when there is no proof, so if witnesses exist, the carrier should just bring them and skip the oath.

keyTerms.meaning: A slope or slippery incline, where falling is not anyone's fault.
Evidence or proof, such as witnesses.
'This works out well' (only in a certain case).
He is exempt (does not have to pay or swear).

phrases.english: And even in the case of a slope too —
phrases.notes: This continues the earlier explanation, which said the oath is about a barrel broken on a slippery slope.

phrases.english: this works out well where there is no evidence,
but where there is evidence —
let him bring evidence and be exempt.

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: תשובה (part of explaining רבי אלעזר's wonder)
steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲפִילּוּ בִּמְקוֹם מִדְרוֹן נָמֵי הֲתִינַח הֵיכָא דְּלֵיכָּא רְאָיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier part of the daf (before this section), which explained רבי אלעזר's wonder under the first approach.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that רבי מאיר's oath applies on a slope.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An oath is only needed when there is no proof. Where witnesses exist, the carrier should bring them and go free with no oath.

steps.title: איסי בן יהודה: no oath when there is an eyewitness
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא as the source that witnesses replace an oath. איסי בן יהודה reads the פסוק 'no one saw… an oath of ה׳ shall be between them' to mean that if someone did see, the שומר brings proof and goes free.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught: איסי בן יהודה says: 'No one saw it; an oath of ה׳ shall be between them.' This implies that if there is someone who saw, he should bring proof and be exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is backing up the previous step with a source. A ברייתא shows that the תורה's oath is only for cases where nobody saw what happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק links the oath to 'no one saw.' איסי בן יהודה learns the flip side: if there is a witness, no oath is needed, and the שומר just brings proof. This supports the claim that the oath in our משנה makes sense only without witnesses.

keyTerms.meaning: 'As it is taught' in a ברייתא; introduces a source.
A תנא who gives the reading of the פסוק here.
An oath of ה׳, the oath of a שומר in the תורה.

steps.whatToRemember: An oath is only for when there is no proof. With witnesses, the שומר brings them and is free, with no oath.

phrases.english: As it is taught: Isi ben Yehuda says:

phrases.aramaic: ״אֵין רֹאֶה שְׁבֻעַת ה׳ תִּהְיֶה בֵּין שְׁנֵיהֶם״,
phrases.english: "No one saw it; an oath of the Lord shall be between them,"
which implies: if there is someone who saw —
he should bring proof and be exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the claim in step 1 that witnesses make an oath unnecessary.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that an oath is not needed when there is evidence.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: איסי בן יהודה reading שמות 22:9–10.

steps.title: ר׳ יוחנן: the oath is an enactment of the Sages
steps.stepSummary: ר׳ חייא בר אבא, quoting ר׳ יוחנן, gives a whole new approach. The carrier's oath is a תקנת חכמים. Without it, nobody would agree to carry a barrel for someone else.
steps.simpleTranslation: ר׳ חייא בר אבא said in the name of ר׳ יוחנן: This oath is an enactment of the Sages. If you do not say so, nobody will carry a barrel for his friend from place to place.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different way to solve the problem with רבי מאיר. The oath is not the regular oath of the תורה; the Sages made it up for the good of society.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, stumbling counts as פשיעה (negligence) according to רבי מאיר, so the carrier should pay. ר׳ יוחנן agrees with that, but says the חכמים let him swear and go free anyway. Otherwise, people would be afraid to carry barrels for others. This removes the need for the slope explanation and its problems.

keyTerms.meaning: An enactment made by the Sages, beyond the basic דין.
'For if you do not say so', introducing the reason for the תקנה.
One who carries something across, from place to place.

steps.whyThisMatters: This changes the oath from a regular oath of the תורה into a rule made by the חכמים. Because of that, the rest of the section rereads רבי יהודה and רבי אלעזר through this lens.
steps.confusionAlert: ר׳ יוחנן is not saying the carrier is innocent by the basic דין. He means that even though the carrier would normally have to pay, the חכמים let him swear and go free.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan:
this oath is an enactment of the Sages,
for if you do not say so —
phrases.notes: He means: if you don't let the carrier swear and go free.

phrases.english: you will have no person who carries a barrel
for his friend from place to place.

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: תירוץ (a new answer to the problem with רבי מאיר)
steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן שְׁבוּעָה זוֹ תַּקָּנַת חֲכָמִים הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the earlier approach (oath on a slope) with a completely different explanation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The carrier's oath is a תקנת חכמים, made so that people will keep carrying things for others.

steps.title: What exactly does he swear?
steps.stepSummary: Under ר׳ יוחנן's approach, the carrier cannot swear that he was not negligent, since stumbling counts as negligence. So the גמרא asks what words his oath uses.
steps.simpleTranslation: How does he swear?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question to set up the next step: what is the exact wording of this oath?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If stumbling counts as פשיעה, the carrier cannot honestly swear 'I was not negligent.' So the oath of the תקנה needs a different wording, and the גמרא asks for it.

phrases.english: How does he swear?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the details of the תקנה from step 3.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact wording of the carrier's oath under the תקנה.

steps.title: רבא: 'I did not break it on purpose'
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the carrier swears that he did not break the barrel on purpose.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: He swears, 'I did not break it on purpose.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question. The oath is that the barrel did not break on purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The carrier cannot swear he was not careless, because stumbling is still carelessness. He can honestly swear it was not deliberate, and the תקנה lets that oath free him.
steps.whatToRemember: Under ר׳ יוחנן's approach, the carrier swears 'I did not break it on purpose,' not 'I was not negligent.'

phrases.english: Rava said:
"An oath that I did not break it on purpose."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא בְּכַוּוֹנָה שְׁבַרְתִּיהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The oath is: 'I did not break it on purpose.'

steps.title: How רבי יהודה fits ר׳ יוחנן's approach
steps.stepSummary: According to ר׳ יוחנן, רבי יהודה does not accept the תקנה. He keeps each שומר at his basic דין: the שומר חנם swears and the שומר שכר pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהודה came to say: A שומר חנם swears and a שומר שכר pays. Each one follows his own regular law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains רבי יהודה's view in the משנה according to ר׳ יוחנן's approach. רבי יהודה wants no special תקנה, just the normal rules for each שומר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By the regular rules, a שומר שכר pays when the barrel breaks from a stumble, and a שומר חנם can swear. רבי יהודה says to leave it that way, with no special תקנה for carrying barrels. So the argument in the משנה is about whether the חכמים made a תקנה.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And came to say', explaining what someone's statement is really teaching.
An unpaid guardian of someone else's object.
A paid guardian (same as שומר שכר).

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda came to say:
an unpaid guardian swears,
a paid guardian pays,
this one according to his law and that one according to his law.
phrases.notes: He means each שומר keeps his normal rule, with no special תקנה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rereads רבי יהודה's view in the משנה through ר׳ יוחנן's approach.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה holds there is no תקנה. Each שומר follows his normal rule.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: the tradition follows רבי מאיר, but he wonders
steps.stepSummary: Under ר׳ יוחנן's approach, רבי אלעזר confirms that there is a tradition following רבי מאיר, meaning the תקנה is real. Still, he wonders how both kinds of שומרים could swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי אלעזר came to say: Yes, there is a tradition like רבי מאיר. However, I wonder whether both this one and that one can swear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rereads רבי אלעזר's statement according to ר׳ יוחנן's approach. He accepts רבי מאיר's ruling as a tradition but still finds it puzzling, which sets up the next two steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר does not reject the תקנה, since he says the tradition is like רבי מאיר. But by normal logic, it is hard to see how both the שומר חנם and the שומר שכר could swear and go free. The next steps explain exactly what puzzles him.

keyTerms.meaning: This one and that one (both kinds of שומר).

steps.confusionAlert: Here the word גמרא does not mean the Talmud. It means 'a tradition I received.'

phrases.english: And Rabbi Elazar came to say:
Yes, there is a tradition in accordance with Rabbi Meir,
but still, I wonder
whether both this one and that one can swear.

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: קשיא (his wonder works like a challenge)
steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲתָא רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר לְמֵימַר אִין גְּמָרָא כְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rereading רבי יהודה, the גמרא now rereads רבי אלעזר through ר׳ יוחנן's approach.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a tradition following רבי מאיר (the תקנה), though רבי אלעזר finds it puzzling that both שומרים can swear.

steps.title: Why would a שומר שכר swear at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the first part of רבי אלעזר's wonder. A שומר חנם can swear he was not negligent. But a שומר שכר pays even without negligence, so what would his oath help?
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that a שומר חנם swears that he was not negligent with it. But a שומר שכר, why does he swear? Even if he was not negligent, he still has to pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out the first problem behind רבי אלעזר's wonder. An oath of 'I was not negligent' cannot free a שומר שכר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שומר חנם only pays for negligence, so swearing 'I was not negligent' frees him. A שומר שכר also pays in cases that are not negligence, like theft and loss, and a stumble is at least that bad. So that oath would not help him at all.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Granted', it makes sense in this case (a problem in another case follows).

phrases.english: Granted, an unpaid guardian —
swears that he was not negligent with it.
But a paid guardian, why does he swear?

phrases.aramaic: כִּי לָא פְּשַׁע נָמֵי בָּעֵי שַׁלּוֹמֵי.
phrases.english: Even when he was not negligent, he must pay.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא שׁוֹמֵר חִנָּם מִשְׁתְּבַע שֶׁלֹּא פָּשַׁע בָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first reason for רבי אלעזר's wonder in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's ruling that a שומר שכר also swears and goes free.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A שומר שכר pays even without negligence, so an oath that he was not negligent cannot free him.

steps.title: Even a שומר חנם: off a slope, how can he swear?
steps.stepSummary: The second part of the wonder: even the שומר חנם's oath only works if the barrel broke on a slope. Anywhere else, stumbling is negligence, so how could he swear he was not negligent?
steps.simpleTranslation: And even a שומר חנם: this works out on a slope. But not on a slope, can he swear that he was not negligent?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the second problem behind רבי אלעזר's wonder. Even the שומר חנם can only swear honestly in a narrow case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי מאיר, stumbling is negligence. Only on a slope is it not the carrier's fault. So in a normal place, the שומר חנם cannot honestly swear 'I was not negligent.' That is why רבי אלעזר wonders how either one can swear, and it explains why the תקנה is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Can he?', a question expecting the answer no.
Not on a slope, in a normal place.

steps.whatToRemember: רבי אלעזר wonders for two reasons. A שומר שכר pays even without negligence. And a שומר חנם can only swear honestly if the barrel broke on a slope.

phrases.english: And even an unpaid guardian too,
this works out well on a slope.
Not on a slope,
can he swear that he was not negligent?
phrases.notes: Off a slope, רבי מאיר counts stumbling as negligence, so this oath would not be true.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲפִילּוּ שׁוֹמֵר חִנָּם נָמֵי הָא תִּינַח בִּמְקוֹם מִדְרוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second problem to step 8. Even the שומר חנם's oath only works in a narrow case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The שומר חנם's oath that he was not negligent.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Stumbling is negligence for רבי מאיר, so off a slope the שומר חנם cannot honestly swear he was not negligent.

steps.title: Even on a slope, why swear if witnesses could be found?
steps.stepSummary: Even if the barrel broke on a slope, an oath only makes sense when there is no evidence. Where evidence is available, the carrier should bring it and be exempt without swearing.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even on a slope, there is still a problem. An oath is fine where there is no evidence. But where there is evidence, he should bring the evidence and be exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a third part to רבי אלעזר's wonder. Even in the one case where the שומר חנם's oath could work (a slope), it should not be needed if witnesses are available.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 limited the oath to a slope. Now the גמרא limits it further: an oath is only for cases where nobody saw what happened. Where witnesses exist, the carrier should bring proof, not swear.

keyTerms.meaning: A slope, where slipping is not considered negligence
This works out fine (only in a limited case)

phrases.english: And even in the case of a slope as well,
phrases.notes: This builds on step 9, where a slope was the only place the שומר חנם could honestly swear.

phrases.english: this works out well where there is no evidence;
but where there is evidence,
let him bring evidence and be exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲפִילּוּ בִּמְקוֹם מִדְרוֹן נָמֵי, הָא תִּינַח הֵיכָא דְּלֵיכָּא רְאָיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the oath even further than step 9: from 'only on a slope' to 'only on a slope with no witnesses available.'
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that, by basic דין, a שומר חנם could swear he was not negligent, even on a slope
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An oath only replaces proof when proof cannot be found. In a place where witnesses are available, the carrier should bring them, so the oath seems unnecessary.

steps.title: איסי בן יהודה's source: no witness means oath, a witness means proof
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes איסי בן יהודה, who reads the פסוק 'with no one seeing, an oath of ה׳ shall be between them' to mean that when there is a witness, the שומר must bring proof and is then exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: איסי בן יהודה says, the פסוק says 'no one sees... an oath of ה׳ shall be between them.' This implies that if someone does see, he should bring proof and be exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source for the rule it just used in step 10. איסי בן יהודה learns from the פסוק that an oath is only for cases with no witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק links the oath to 'no one sees.' איסי reads that link strictly: if someone did see, the case is settled by proof, not by an oath. This is the source behind the challenge in step 10.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is taught in a ברייתא
A תנא whose reading of the פסוק is the basis here
There is no one who sees (no witness)
An oath in the name of ה׳

phrases.english: As it is taught: איסי בן יהודה says:
"there is no one who sees,
an oath of ה׳ shall be between them"
which implies: if there is someone who sees,
let him bring evidence and be exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the ברייתא that supports the rule used in the challenge of step 10.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that where witnesses exist, a שומר brings proof instead of swearing
steps.raayaSupportSource: איסי בן יהודה's reading of 'אין רואה שבועת ה׳ תהיה בין שניהם' (שמות 22:9–10)

steps.title: The broken barrel in the market of מחוזא
steps.stepSummary: A man broke a barrel of wine on a protruding ledge in the busy market of מחוזא. רבא told him that since people are always there, he must bring witnesses and then he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man was carrying a barrel of wine in the market of מחוזא and broke it on a ledge in מחוזא. He came before רבא. רבא said: the market of מחוזא is full of people. Go bring proof and you will be exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story where רבא actually applies איסי's rule. A barrel broke in a crowded market, so רבא requires witnesses instead of an oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the market is always busy, someone surely saw the accident. So the carrier cannot simply swear. He must bring witnesses that it was an accident, and then he is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: A ledge or protrusion sticking out from a wall

phrases.english: A certain man
who was transporting a barrel of wine
in the marketplace of מחוזא,
and broke it on a protrusion in מחוזא.
He came before רבא.
He said to him:
The marketplace of מחוזא, people are commonly found there;
go, bring evidence and be exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דַּהֲוָה קָא מְעַבַּר חָבִיתָא דְחַמְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the theory of איסי's rule to a real case where רבא applies it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An accident in a busy public place requires witnesses, not an oath, and with witnesses the carrier is exempt.

steps.title: רב יוסף asks: Are you ruling like איסי?
steps.stepSummary: רבא's son רב יוסף asks whose opinion this ruling follows, and suggests it follows איסי בן יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף, his son, said to him: Whose opinion is this? איסי's?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא's son asks him to name the source of his ruling. This sets up רבא's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Requiring proof instead of an oath matches איסי's reading of the פסוק. רב יוסף wants to know whether רבא really holds like איסי's opinion.

phrases.english: רב יוסף, his son, said to him:
In accordance with whom? Like איסי?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יוֹסֵף בְּרֵיהּ: כְּמַאן כְּאִיסִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of רבא's ruling in step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רבא's ruling is based on איסי בן יהודה's opinion

steps.title: רבא: Yes, like איסי, and that is our הלכה
steps.stepSummary: רבא confirms that he ruled like איסי and says that we hold like him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Yes, like איסי, and we hold like him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers his son. He agrees that his ruling follows איסי, and he says this is the הלכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא is not just quoting a minority view. He says איסי's opinion is the accepted ruling, so a שומר who could bring witnesses must bring them.

keyTerms.meaning: We hold like him (this is the halacha)

phrases.english: He said to him: Yes, like איסי,
and we hold in accordance with him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִין כְּאִיסִי, וּסְבִירָא לַן כְּווֹתֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב יוסף's question in step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ruling follows איסי, and the הלכה follows איסי.

steps.title: The four hundred jugs of wine that went sour
steps.stepSummary: A man asked his friend to buy him 400 jugs of wine. The friend bought them and later reported that the wine had gone sour.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man said to his friend: Go buy me four hundred jugs of wine. He went and bought them for him. Later he came to him and said: I bought you four hundred jugs of wine, and they went sour.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a second story. This step only lays out the facts, and רבא's ruling comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The friend claims the loss was not his fault, since the wine went bad. The question will be whether he can just claim this, or whether he must prove it.

keyTerms.meaning: They turned sour (the wine went bad)

phrases.english: A certain man who said to his friend:
Go buy for me
four hundred jugs of wine.
He went and bought them for him.
In the end he came before him and said to him:

phrases.aramaic: זְבִינֵי לָךְ אַרְבַּע מְאָה דַּנֵּי חַמְרָא
phrases.english: I bought you four hundred jugs of wine
and they turned sour.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ לְחַבְרֵיהּ: זִיל זְבֵין לִי אַרְבַּע מְאָה דַּנֵּי חַמְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a second story that will also apply איסי's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the facts: the buyer claims the wine soured on its own.

steps.title: רבא: Something this big gets known, so bring proof
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that 400 jugs of wine going sour would become widely known. So the buyer must prove the wine was good when he bought it, and then he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: He came before רבא. רבא said to him: When four hundred jugs of wine go sour, the matter becomes known. Go bring proof that at the start, when you bought them, the wine was good, and you will be exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא rules on the second story. Since such a big event would be known publicly, the buyer cannot just make a claim. He must bring proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is איסי's rule again, applied to something people hear about instead of something people see. Because proof is available, the buyer must show the wine was good at purchase. That shows he did not buy bad wine, and then he is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter has a voice: people hear about it

phrases.english: He came before רבא, who said to him:
Four hundred jugs of wine turning sour,
the matter has a voice;
phrases.notes: He means people would surely hear about it, so witnesses can be found.

phrases.english: go, bring evidence
that originally, when you bought them,
it was good wine, and be exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַרְבַּע מְאָה דַּנֵּי חַמְרָא תְּקִיפִי קָלָא אִית לַהּ לְמִילְּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבא's ruling on the facts from step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Where an event would be publicly known, the claimant must bring proof (that the wine was good at purchase), and then he is exempt.

steps.title: רב יוסף asks again: Like איסי?
steps.stepSummary: Once more רב יוסף asks whether this ruling follows איסי בן יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף, his son, said to him: Whose opinion is this? איסי's?
steps.whatsHappening: The same question as in the first story. רב יוסף checks whether this ruling also follows איסי, and the answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא repeats the exchange word for word. This shows that the same rule of איסי applies even when the proof comes from the matter being publicly known.

phrases.english: רב יוסף, his son, said to him:
In accordance with whom? Like איסי?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יוֹסֵף בְּרֵיהּ: כְּמַאן כְּאִיסִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of רבא's ruling in step 16, just as in step 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the second ruling also follows איסי בן יהודה

steps.title: רבא confirms again: We hold like איסי
steps.stepSummary: רבא again answers that he ruled like איסי, and that the הלכה follows איסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Yes, like איסי, and we hold like him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the same answer as before. This closes both stories with a clear הלכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two separate cases end with the same answer. This makes it clear that איסי's rule is accepted: when proof is available, a person cannot rely on an oath or a bare claim.
steps.whatToRemember: Following איסי בן יהודה: an oath is only for cases where no one could know what happened. If witnesses or public knowledge are available, the שומר must bring proof, and then he is exempt. רבא rules this way as the הלכה.

phrases.english: He said to him: Yes, like איסי,
and we hold in accordance with him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִין כְּאִיסִי, וּסְבִירָא לַן כְּווֹתֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 17 and repeats the conclusion from step 14.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The הלכה follows איסי: where proof is available, one must bring proof instead of swearing, and with that proof he is exempt.

steps.title: A rule for porters who carry with a pole
steps.stepSummary: רב חייא בר יוסף made a rule (תקנה) in סיכרא: porters who carry with a pole and break the item pay half its value.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חייא בר יוסף made a rule in סיכרא: porters who carry loads on a pole and break them must pay half.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a community rule about porters who break the item they are carrying with a pole. They pay half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now we saw רבא's rulings about a carrier who broke something. Here a local Sage sets a fixed compromise: half payment. It is not full liability and not full exemption.

keyTerms.meaning: He made a תקנה, a rule set up for the community
A carrying pole, here one used by a single porter

phrases.aramaic: אַתְקֵין רַב חִיָּיא בַּר יוֹסֵף בְּסִיכְרָא:
phrases.english: Rav Chiyya bar Yosef made a rule in Sikhra:
those who carry with a pole, and it breaks,
must pay half.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתְקֵין רַב חִיָּיא בַּר יוֹסֵף בְּסִיכְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of a carrier who breaks what he carries, now with a local rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Pole-carriers who break the load pay half.

steps.title: Why only half?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the half-payment rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the payment is exactly half. This sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A carrier normally pays either in full (if he was careless) or nothing (if it was an accident). A half-payment needs a reason.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the rule in step 19.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason for a half payment.

steps.title: Halfway between accident and carelessness
steps.stepSummary: A pole load is too much for one person and too little for two, so a break is equally close to an accident (אונס) and to carelessness (פשיעה).
steps.simpleTranslation: It is too much for one person and too little for two, so it is close to an accident and close to carelessness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that this kind of load sits right in the middle. So the break counts as half accident and half carelessness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The load is heavy for one porter, so a break looks a bit like carelessness. But hiring two would be too much for such a load, so it also looks like an accident. Since the case is evenly balanced, they split the loss.

phrases.english: it is too much for one and too little for two,
close to an accident and close to negligence.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The case is balanced between accident and negligence, so the loss is split.

steps.title: With a two-person carrying tool he pays in full
steps.stepSummary: If he carried the load with a דיגלא, a tool meant for double loads, he pays the full amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: With a דיגלא, he pays all of it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a contrasting case. A porter using a tool built for heavy, double loads pays in full.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A דיגלא shows that he took on a load meant for two people. Carrying that alone is real carelessness (פשיעה), so the half-compromise does not apply.

keyTerms.meaning: A wooden carrying tool made for double loads
All of it, the full amount

phrases.english: With a digla, he pays all of it.

steps.whatToRemember: Pole load (between one and two people) = pay half. Double-load tool (דיגלא) = pay in full.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the contrasting case where the half rule does not apply.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Using a דיגלא counts as negligence, so he pays in full.

steps.title: Porters break רבה בר בר חנן's wine barrel
steps.stepSummary: Porters broke רבה בר בר חנן's barrel of wine. He took their cloaks, and they went to complain to רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some porters broke a barrel of wine of רבה בר בר חנן. He took their cloaks. They came and told רב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story about porters who broke a barrel. This sets the scene for רב's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה בר בר חנן took the cloaks as payment for his loss. The story will test whether a victim should press his rights against poor workers.

phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Chanan:

phrases.aramaic: תְּבַרוּ לֵיהּ הָנְהוּ שָׁקוֹלָאֵי חָבִיתָא דְחַמְרָא,
phrases.english: certain porters broke his barrel of wine,
he took their cloaks.
They came and told Rav.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָן תְּבַרוּ לֵיהּ הָנְהוּ שָׁקוֹלָאֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story on the same topic of carriers who break items.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Case setup: porters broke a barrel and their cloaks were taken.

steps.title: רב: give them back their cloaks
steps.stepSummary: רב tells רבה בר בר חנן to return the porters' cloaks.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said to him: Give them their cloaks.
steps.whatsHappening: רב rules that the cloaks must be given back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the earlier rulings, the porters might owe for the loss. רב still tells רבה בר בר חנן to give up his security.

phrases.english: He said to him: Give them their cloaks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רב responds to the porters' complaint.

steps.title: Is that really the law?
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנן asks רב whether this is the actual law.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Is this the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר בר חנן is surprised and asks whether the law really requires this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He suspects the strict law is on his side. So he asks what the basis for the ruling is.

phrases.english: He said to him: Is this the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions רב's ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether returning the cloaks is required by law.

steps.title: Yes: walk in the way of good people
steps.stepSummary: רב answers yes, quoting "so that you walk in the way of good people", and רבה בר בר חנן returns the cloaks.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Yes, "so that you may walk in the way of good people." He gave them their cloaks.
steps.whatsHappening: רב grounds his ruling in a פסוק, and רבה בר בר חנן obeys.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source is not ordinary damages law but a פסוק about how good people behave. For a person like רבה בר בר חנן, this standard counts as "the law."

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִין, ״לְמַעַן תֵּלֵךְ בְּדֶרֶךְ טוֹבִים״.
phrases.english: He said to him: Yes, "so that you may walk in the way of good people."
He gave them their cloaks.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אִין לְמַעַן תֵּלֵךְ בְּדֶרֶךְ טוֹבִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבה בר בר חנן's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes, based on the פסוק about walking in the way of good people.

steps.title: The porters plead: we are poor and hungry
steps.stepSummary: The porters tell רב that they are poor, worked all day, are hungry, and have nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: We are poor, we worked hard all day, we are hungry, and we have nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The porters ask for more than their cloaks. This sets up רב's next ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Getting their cloaks back is not enough. They describe their poverty and their wasted day of work to ask for their wages too.

phrases.english: They said to him: We are poor,
and we toiled all day,
and we are hungry, and we have nothing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The porters raise a further request.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The porters ask for help with their need.

steps.title: רב: pay them their wages
steps.stepSummary: רב tells רבה בר בר חנן to go and pay the porters their wages.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Go, give them their wages.
steps.whatsHappening: רב rules that רבה בר בר חנן must also pay the porters their wages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now רב goes even further. Besides not collecting for the broken barrel, the owner pays for the job the porters failed to finish properly.

phrases.english: He said to him: Go give them their wages.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רב responds to the porters' plea.

steps.title: Again: is that really the law?
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנן again asks whether this is the law.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Is this the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר בר חנן asks the same question a second time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Paying wages to people who caused him a loss seems even further from the strict law. So he checks again.

phrases.english: He said to him: Is this the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the second ruling.

steps.title: Yes: keep the paths of the righteous
steps.stepSummary: רב answers yes, quoting the second half of the פסוק, "and keep the paths of the righteous."
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Yes, "and keep the paths of the righteous."
steps.whatsHappening: רב finishes the פסוק to support his second ruling, and the story ends.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first half of the פסוק led to returning the cloaks. The second half leads to the further step of paying wages. Together they show a standard of behavior above the strict law.
steps.whatToRemember: Even when the law might let you collect, a good and righteous person may be expected to give up his claim. He may even help poor workers who caused him a loss.
steps.confusionAlert: This story does not cancel the earlier rules about carriers paying for damage. It shows what רב expected of a person like רבה בר בר חנן beyond those rules.

phrases.english: He said to him: Yes, "and keep the paths of the righteous."
phrases.notes: משלי ב:כ, the second half of the same פסוק רב quoted before.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the second question and closes the story.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Based on the פסוק, a righteous person returns the cloaks and pays the wages.

steps.title: Hadran: closing פרק השוכר את האומנין
steps.stepSummary: The chapter השוכר את האומנין comes to an end.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, השוכר את האומנין.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the closing line of the chapter about hiring craftsmen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הדרן marks the end of the chapter. A new chapter begins right after it.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you, the formula for finishing a chapter

phrases.english: We will return to you, "One who hires craftsmen".

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the chapter.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: End of the chapter השוכר את האומנין.

steps.title: New משנה: an employer can't force early starts or late finishes
steps.stepSummary: In a place where workers don't usually start early or stay late, an employer cannot force them to.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone hires workers and tells them to come early and stay late, in a place where the custom is not to do so, he cannot force them.
steps.whatsHappening: A new chapter begins with a משנה about workers' hours. They follow the local custom, not the employer's demand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the employer says so at the time of hiring, local custom sets the default work day. The workers cannot be made to go beyond it.

keyTerms.meaning: To start early and to stay late

phrases.english: MISHNAH: One who hires workers
and told them to come early and stay late,
in a place where the custom is not to come early
and not to stay late,
he is not allowed to force them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the new chapter.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An employer cannot force workers beyond the local custom of working hours.

steps.title: Food and treats also follow local custom
steps.stepSummary: Where the custom is to feed workers or give them sweets, the employer must do so. Everything follows the local custom.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where the custom is to feed them, he must feed them. Where the custom is to give sweets, he must give them. Everything follows the custom of the place.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה extends the idea to food. It then states a general rule: local custom decides the terms of work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first case protected workers from extra hours. This case gives them benefits that the custom provides. The closing line turns both into one principle: מנהג המדינה.
steps.whatToRemember: In hiring workers, the local custom (מנהג המדינה) sets hours, food, and other terms.

phrases.english: In a place where the custom is to feed, he must feed;
to provide sweets, he must provide;
everything follows the custom of the place.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה with more cases and the general rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All terms of hiring follow מנהג המדינה.

steps.title: The son promises the workers food
steps.stepSummary: The משנה tells a story: רבי יוחנן בן מתיא sent his son to hire workers, and the son promised to give them food.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a story with רבי יוחנן בן מתיא. He told his son: Go hire workers for us. The son went and agreed to give them food.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה starts a story to show how the rule about feeding workers works in real life. This step sets up the problem the father will point out next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The son promised food but did not say how much or what kind. That open-ended promise is the problem the story is built around.

keyTerms.meaning: Agreed to, set as a term of the deal

phrases.english: There was an incident with Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Matya
who said to his son:
Go out and hire workers for us.
He went and agreed to provide them with food.
phrases.notes: He promised them meals but never said what kind or how much.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real-life story that illustrates the rule from Step 33 about feeding workers.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The setup case: food was promised to workers without any limits.

steps.title: The father warns that the promise has no limit
steps.stepSummary: The father says even a feast like שלמה's would not be enough for these workers, so his son must set a limit before they begin: only bread and legumes.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the son came back to his father, the father said: My son, even if you made them a feast like King שלמה's, you would not have done what you owe them, because they are children of אברהם, יצחק and יעקב. So before they start working, go tell them: This is on condition that all you can claim from me is bread and legumes.
steps.whatsHappening: The father explains why an open promise of food is dangerous. He tells his son to set a clear limit before the work begins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since these workers are children of the אבות, an unlimited promise of food could mean they deserve the very best, with no end. Adding the condition before work starts turns the promise into the simple, normal workers' meal of bread and legumes.

keyTerms.meaning: King שלמה's royal feast, the most lavish meal possible
Bread and legumes, a simple workers' meal

steps.confusionAlert: The father is not saying workers must always get a royal feast. He means that an open-ended promise could be read that way, so the son should limit it.

phrases.english: And when he came to his father,
he said to him: My son,
even if you make for them
a feast like that of Solomon in his time,
you would not fulfill your obligation to them,
since they are descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Rather, before they begin the work,
go out and say to them:
on condition that you have no claim on me
except for bread and legumes alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the son's open-ended promise from Step 34.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An unlimited promise of food could be endless, so the employer should set a limit (bread and legumes) before the work starts.

steps.title: Local custom decides, so no condition was needed
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says the son did not need to add any condition, because everything follows local custom.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: He did not need to say this, because everything follows the custom of the place.
steps.whatsHappening: A second תנא disagrees with the father's advice. He says a promise of food automatically means the usual local workers' meal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father worried that "food" had no limit. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says it already has a limit: whatever is normal in that place. So no extra condition is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who disagrees with the father's approach
The local custom of the place

steps.whatToRemember: The father says an open promise of food needs a stated limit. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says local custom already sets the limit.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
He did not need to say this;
everything follows the custom of the place.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: לֹא הָיָה צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the father's advice in Step 35.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No condition is needed, since a promise of food automatically follows local custom.

steps.title: Why does the משנה need to teach this?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins by asking why the משנה needed to say an employer cannot force workers to start early and stay late. Isn't that obvious?
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Isn't this obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the first rule of the משנה and challenges it as too obvious to need saying. This sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Where local custom is not to start early or stay late, of course the employer cannot demand it. So the גמרא wants to know what new thing the משנה is teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that explains the משנה

phrases.english: GEMARA: Isn't it obvious!
phrases.notes: This goes back to the first line of the משנה: an employer can't force workers to start early or stay late.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the גמרא by returning to the משנה's first rule (Step 32).
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that an employer cannot force workers to start early and stay late.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Where that is not the custom, the employer obviously has no right to demand it, so the rule seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Higher pay buys better work, not longer hours
steps.stepSummary: The rule is needed for a case where the employer paid above the normal wage. Even then, the workers can say the extra pay was for better work, not longer hours.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the rule is needed where he gave them higher wages. You might think he could tell them: I raised your pay so that you would start early and stay late for me. So the משנה teaches us that they can answer: You raised our pay so that we would do good-quality work for you.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question by finding a case where the rule is not obvious: the employer paid extra.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Higher pay might seem to give the employer a claim to more hours. The משנה teaches that the workers can say the extra money was for better quality work. So the employer still cannot force them to work longer than the local custom.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for a case where
You would start early and stay late

steps.whatToRemember: Even with extra pay, an employer cannot force longer hours than the local custom. Higher pay can be explained as payment for better work.
steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that extra pay with no stated purpose does not let the employer change the custom on working hours.

phrases.english: No, it is needed where he increased their wages.
You might have said that he can say to them:
The fact that I increased your wages
was with the understanding that you would start early and stay late with me;
so it teaches us that they can say to him:
What you added for us
was with the understanding that we would do good-quality work for you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'it's obvious' challenge of Step 37.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (לא צריכא): the rule applies even where the wages were raised.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the employer paid extra, he could demand early starts and late finishes.
steps.terutzMaskana: The workers can claim the extra pay was for better quality work, so he still cannot force longer hours.
